commentBody: Pretty good
Excellent challenge, snapped together artfully like a good puzzle should.

Wow.  Now that was a Friday!

Other than some sports trivia that even my sports-obsessed husband didn't know, I thought every clue was tough but gettable.

I always enjoy a puzzle where the first pass makes it feel impossible, but bit by bit I can get a foothold here and there, and after several more passes, I'm rewarded with the happy music.

Great puzzle!
Was certain I'd have many mistakes to hunt down, but my guesses were unusually lucky today.
Good puzzle. I'll admit I was not aware of Ooh Aah Point -- but I am now.

I got a late start, but this took me much longer than Fridays have been taking me lately, and it provided the perfect extended Friday NYT puzzle experience. Everything took me a long time this evening, but the time spent was well rewarded with a tightly constructed, very clever puzzle. This got solved little by little only after I kept returning over and over to the same unsolved areas. Very satisfying to finally solve a puzzle that stayed unsolved for so long.

"It’s got “I should know this” trivia."

Not in my book.  OOHAAHPOINT, EMILE and SLOANE, etc are not "I should know this" trivia.  There are a lot of proper nouns in this puzzle.

When I wrote my Travelogue, I came up with a term called a "Grand Canyon Moment" and associated "Grand Canyon Theory."

The short of it is, the value you get from staring at something like the Grand Canyon decreases at an exponential scale. I posited that 90% of the value you get from seeing the Grand Canyon comes in the first 30 seconds and 99% in the first five minutes.

I went in 2001 and am going back next month. I booked the in park lodge because the one thing I most remember about the Grand Canyon was that feeling of pure joy when I woke up in the lodge and ran to the rim first thing in the morning to see the view. I think the scale resets after 25 years...
So much unfamiliarity for us but it slowly came together. We'd like to think that means it was well-clued.  Much appreciation here.

Also, musicians in the crowd, is "la ti do" considered to be the notes A, B, and C?  I thought they do-re-mi thing was to avoid a particular key. Couldn't it just as easily be "D sharp, F, F sharp"?

"Kagemusha,"in 1980, was my introduction to KUROSAWA. At the movie theater, I sat between my brother and a stranger, a Japanese man. I stole glimpses of both of their faces throughout the movie, looking for direction because I felt lost. Whenever my brother was serious, the Japanese man smiled; when the Japanese man was serious, my brother was smiling. That's when I deeply understood, at 16, that there was something intrinsically different in our cultures. No wonder I was lost. That's the indelible mark the movie left on me. That and a most traumatizing scene of horses on a battlefield falling over in slow motion, struggling to stand back up, or succumbing and dying. Gut-wrenching. In brighter news, today I was able to resist my self-doubt and bad habit of doing "check puzzle" halfway through a Friday solve. To my surprise, I gold starred without having to flyspeck! But I don't feel smug because all credit goes to Mr. Robles Ojeda for creating a puzzle that was crunchy but doable, inspiring me to keep going even through uncertainty. Thank you! (Capping it off with RadioHEAD... https://youtu.be/yudEj4W1TjU?is=0SyQhPscFN2ayyhv ...and AHMAD Jamal for the jazz lovers: https://youtu.be/SiARr9JhLEo?is=k9y9NP7O_UbIzG13)

For those commenters uncomfortable with too much French in the puzzle, I think that 42A [Étendue bleue] is a nice turn of phrase. It means something like "blue expanse." Etendue means stretched out, sort of. I knew it meant "sea" or "sky": MER for "sea" in French.

By the way, La MER is feminine in French. (All nouns are either feminine or masculine.) Therefore, the adjective "bleue" has the added "e" to make it feminine. As noted in a recent comments section, the adjective "bleue" follows the noun here.

In addition, 20D [Paris's Champs-___] ELYSEES is a really nice place. A broad tree-lined avenue leading to the Arc de Triomphe, one of the spokes of the wheel in that spectacular grid. The boulevard is lined with some of the most elegant stores of the city. I visited The American Drugstore there, right near the Arc. Vive la France.

I still had more white space than any puzzle in recent memory. But, it’s finally done and I feel pretty good about that.

TIL I’m from a “movable do” country so I was vexed by 5D. Why must the notes be A, B, and C? Musical theory taught me that do was the first note of the scale, any scale. Apparently in “fixed do” countries, do is always C. Doh!

A fantastic puzzle, one of the most enjoyable for me this year. I completed it quite quickly, in 9:38, which is only one second away from my Friday PB, but I do not think it was easy - rather, it was one of those puzzles where the wavelength really clicked for me, and many of the answers I knew from obscure but indelible places. Having visited the Grand Canyon in 2017, OOHAAHPOINT has always stuck in my mind because I found it quite humorous when we stumbled upon it, and fellow Australians will understand when I reference a certain fast bowler named Glenn McGrath. Being a fan of his, I’ve always recalled it. The Dylan Thomas poem was familiar to me and the answer a gimme, but only because of a recent reading by a certain UK comedian, Diane Morgan, on the series “Last One Laughing”, which once seen, can not be easily forgotten - if you have not seen that, do yourself a favour, but prepare to potentially be in pain from laughing, (if that’s your kind of thing) - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_s3nK3p9YG0 I’m a zythophile, so AMBERALES was great; as a secondary school teacher, I hear the term CRASHINGOUT at least every second day; I teach music so ABC was simple; BOOTYCALLS was hilarious and genius; everything just clicked today. An all-round great puzzle, thank you Adryel!

So, in solfège--the musical practice of singing syllables to notes--there are two main methods: "fixed do," in which "do" is always C, no matter what key one is singing in, and "movable do," in which "la ti do" (or "la si ut") are the last three notes of a major scale, no matter in which key it is. Unfortunately, I learned the latter, so [La ti do] meant, well, la ti do, since MINOR THIRD ain't gonna fit in three letters. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solf%C3%A8ge#Modern_use In musicology at least, the distinction between "baroque" and "rococo" is a rather vague one. I'm not sure Sylvius Leopold Weiss would count as rococo, but the Villa Zilari certainly does: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WEIDLFusTYg&list=RDWEIDLFusTYg&start_radio=1 Nancy J., below, already beat me to Beck.

Is no one going to point out that scones are more typically served at afternoon (or low) tea? High tea is the equivalent of supper. Americans persust in the belief that the "high" in "high tea" means "classy." It refers to the height of the table. Afternoon tea is served to the Dowager Countess and her guests in the sitting room at low tables. High tea is served at the kitchen table.
